There are two distinct American authors often confused due to their nearly identical names. Thomas Wolfe lived from 1900 to 1938, and Tom Wolfe lived from 1930 to 2018. Their different generations, styles, and career paths frequently lead to mix-ups in academic and cultural contexts.

Thomas Wolfe came first. He was born in Asheville, North Carolina, and published four major novels including Look Homeward, Angel. He died young at thirty-seven from tuberculosis. His work is introspective modernist autobiography. His editor was Maxwell Perkins, the legendary editor also famous for working with Hemingway and Fitzgerald. Perkins heavily revised Wolfe's sprawling manuscripts.

Tom Wolfe was born decades later and became famous as a journalist and innovator of what was called New Journalism—a stylized nonfiction form blending literary techniques with reportage. The Right Stuff and Bonfire of the Vanities are his most famous works. Tom Wolfe's breakthrough was journalism and cultural criticism in the nineteen-sixties and seventies, with essays on Las Vegas, astronauts, and American excess. He didn't turn to traditional novels until later in his career.

Thomas Wolfe's work emphasizes memory, loss, and the impossibility of returning home. His posthumous novel was titled You Can't Go Home Again, and that phrase has become famous. Tom Wolfe's satire, by contrast, skewers American materialism, social climbing, and radical chic. It is a completely different thematic and tonal register from Thomas Wolfe's earnest romanticism.
